paras: The lynching of John Winn took place around midnight of April 27-28, 1881, when a masked mob of thirty to forty men entered the jail at Paris, Kentucky, and shot Winn dead in his cell. Winn was being held under indictment for the murder of William Moreland, a young man of Bourbon County. A coroner's jury found that he had been killed by persons unknown, and the story ran in papers from Washington to Kansas.

William Moreland was shot and killed near Talbott Station in Bourbon County on the night of February 27, 1881, and Winn, who managed the farm owned by Moreland's mother, was arrested for the killing. According to a Paris dispatch to the Cincinnati Gazette, Moreland's mother had refused him entry to the house, saying she feared trouble with Winn, and Winn fired through a window. Winn claimed he had heard Moreland say "Come on, boys, now let's go for him" and fired in fear of an attack, while the National Republican said he shot from ambush as Moreland rode past.

Within days Winn was released, by one account for insufficient evidence and by another after a plea of insanity at the examining trial. He was rearrested with his brother Dennis and Mrs. Moreland, who gave bail of $3,000, and the Bourbon County grand jury indicted him for murder. A Paris special to the Louisville Commercial reported that the opinion that the accused "would ultimately escape justice" had become general.

Late on Wednesday night, April 27, masked men came to the Paris jail claiming to have prisoners in charge. Once let in, they demanded the Winns; Jailer McCarney refused to give up the keys, and the National Republican said he held them off for an hour. His wife, fearing for his life, handed over the keys, though the Courier-Journal special said the jailer himself gave them up.

Ordered out of his cell, Winn refused and seized a chair to defend himself. The mob fired seven shots by one count, five of which struck him, and he died almost at once. Lizzie Mattson, described as a "colored woman" in the next cell, said a large man fired first, and a masked man threatened to shoot her if she kept watching. Dennis Winn, held fifteen feet away, was not disturbed, and the mob rode away while an armed guard kept the jailer from raising the alarm.

Magistrate J. M. Daniels, acting as coroner, removed the body the next morning and held an inquest, whose jury found that Winn was killed by shots fired by persons unknown. Winn's father demanded letters thought to be from Mrs. Moreland and threatened the coroner, who fined him and meant to use the letters against her. The Kentucky Gazette later reported that the letters had been found on Winn's body, that Mrs. Moreland was out on a new bond, and that a rumor of her hanging at Cynthiana was untrue. No report of an arrest of any member of the mob appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press through at least three Paris dispatches, to the Louisville Courier-Journal, the Louisville Commercial and the National Republican, and through the local True Kentuckian, reprinted in the Lexington Kentucky Gazette. Headlines ranged from "A Cowardly K[entucky] Mob" in the National Republican to "Mob Violence" in the Wheeling Register and "Mob Murder in Kentucky" in the Weekly Union Times. The Kentucky Gazette headed its report "Shot and Killed In Our Jail" and had earlier called for the gallows to replace private killings.

Crime-column briefs through early May in Wisconsin, Missouri and Kansas named Winn as "a murderer" or "a Kentucky murderer," and the Watertown Republican said the mob had come "in order to lynch him." One Savannah brief garbled the name as "John Wend." No paper in the coverage gave Winn's race.

Accounts differ on the size of the mob, given as thirty by the National Republican and about forty by the Commercial special and the True Kentuckian, while a night-watchman was said to have sworn to a far larger number. They also differ on the hour and on the number of shots fired.

reader.title: Lynching of John Winn
bases: A masked, mounted mob of thirty to forty men entered the Paris jail at night and shot John Winn dead in his cell while he was held on a murder charge (A7, A8, A14).

Winn was shot dead in jail by a mob of thirty (A8) or about forty (A7, A14) men acting without authority, after the opinion had become general that the accused 'would ultimately escape justice' (A7). The papers do not state Winn's race, so whether this belongs among anti-Black lynchings is not shown.

Separate Paris dispatches to the Louisville Commercial (A7) and Courier-Journal (A9, A10), a Paris dispatch in the National Republican (A8), and the Paris True Kentuckian as reprinted in Lexington (A14, A15) agree that a mob shot Winn dead in his cell.

framing.detail: Headlined 'A Cowardly Kentucky Mob' (OCR 'A Cowardly KViitticIfy 3Iob'), after heading the February killing 'The Usual Kentucky Murders'.
Regional papers treated it as another Kentucky killing, with heads such as 'Another Kentucky Tragedy' (OCR 'ANOTHER KENTUCKY TKAQKDY') and 'Shot and Killed In Our Jail'.
Crime-column briefs across the Midwest called Winn 'a murderer' or 'a Kentucky murderer' and named the mob plainly.
